entry.title: Will ‘You Can See Everything’ Catch ‘Fahrenheit 9/11’ to Be the Highest-Grossing Documentary Ever?
entry.summary: 'You Can See Everything' is breaking records for a documentary at the box office, but it has a long way to catch Michael Moore's 'Fahrenheit 9/11.'
entry.content:
It’s too early to say if Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “You Can See Everything” will win Oscars or have a direct impact on history as it pertains to Elizabeth Holmes and Theranos, but it does feel like a movie that journalists are going to be referencing for a long time as a significant benchmark for documentary films at the box office.

Currently sitting at $45.1 million domestic, with no international release to speak of yet, A24’s film is already one of the highest-grossing documentaries ever. Domestically (not factoring inflation) it has already placed firmly within the top 10 and has obliterated films like “Free Solo” ($17.5 million), “Won’t You Be My Neighbor” ($22.8 million), and “An Inconvenient Truth” ($24.1 million). It has surpassed some big nature docs like “Earth,” “Chimpanzee,” and lags only “March of the Penguins” ($77.4 million), and it has surpassed concert docs like “Katy Perry: Part of Me” ($25.3 million) and “One Direction: This Is Us” ($28.8 million) but lags the Michael Jackson doc “This Is It” ($72 million) and “Justin Bieber: Never Say Never” ($73 million).

Related Stories
‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game
‘I Play Rocky’ Wins Virginia Film Fest Audience Award as Peter Farrelly’s Stallone Drama Readies for Theaters

If we want to put a bunch of really dumb caveats and qualifiers on it, “You Can See Everything” is already domestically the highest-grossing non-concert, non-political, non-nature docs ever made, a made-up distinction previously held, by my count, by “Won’t You Be My Neighbor?” (sorry Mister Rogers).

But even if it passes all those other movies, it might still fall short of the documentary that remains far and away the biggest box office hit for a doc ever, Michael Moore‘s 2004 film “Fahrenheit 9/11,” Moore’s scathing takedown of President Bush and the Iraq War as released in the heat of a massive election year.

Moore’s film did not win the Oscar (though it did win the Palme D’Or at Cannes) because it was ineligible after airing on TV ahead of the election, and it did not prevent George W. Bush from being re-elected to a second term, and it probably isn’t even Moore’s best film. But it’s worth remembering just how seismic an event the film was upon its release, not unlike the stir that initial cryptic, meme-worthy teaser of Fielder and Holmes was.

Moore was already a firebrand with instant name recognition thanks to “Bowling for Columbine,” which was previously among the highest-grossing documentaries ever. But “Fahrenheit 9/11” carried with it even more publicity and attention, including because of the fight to get it to screens in the first place. Disney famously blocked Harvey and Bob Weinstein’s Miramax from releasing “Fahrenheit 9/11,” leading the Weinsteins to buy the film back and then partner with Lions Gate and IFC Films to get the movie into theaters. It even had to do so within an incredibly quick turnaround time of 24 days to get prints made and get the film delivered to theaters. Even then, Lions Gate co-president Tom Ortenberg was predicting that the film was going to disrupt distribution and set the record as the biggest documentary ever.

He was right. “Fahrenheit 9/11” opened on just 868 screens on June 25, but it was the No. 1 movie in America with $23.9 million, beating out other new releases like “White Chicks” and “The Notebook.” “You Can See Everything” opened to a similar number of theaters but made only $15.6 million in that first weekend. By July 4 weekend it had expanded to nearly double the theaters and made another $22 million, and by its fifth weekend was over $100 million. The film ultimately played in theaters for 15 weeks into October ahead of the election. Domestically, it made $119.1 million and even made an additional $103 million abroad to bring its worldwide total to $222.4 million. “This Is It” actually has the edge worldwide with $267.9 million, but the bulk of that came from overseas audiences.

The film sparked serious headlines about whether it would damage Bush in the election, and it was a big enough media sensation that “Fahrenheit 451” author Ray Bradbury lashed out at Moore as a “jerk.” Other filmmakers had released parody documentaries against Moore, and it earned sharp criticisms from political pundits disputing its accuracy. Moore’s follow-up movie “Sicko” received an even larger budget of $9 million from the Weinsteins, and it too grossed above “Bowling for Columbine” with $24.5 million domestic.

Clearly the conditions under which documentaries are released in theaters have changed drastically since “Fahrenheit 9/11.” Such a film would most likely today open on streaming, and in today’s hyper-polarized political climate, might struggle to be platformed by gun-shy distributors and streamers. And the market for all documentaries in theaters has fallen drastically in the post-Covid era. “Melania” was previously the highest-grossing doc of 2026 with $16.6 million domestic, but that one is an outlier for a number of reasons.

For “You Can See Everything” to catch “Fahrenheit 9/11,” it would have to put up “Obsession” levels of word of mouth, continually notching up at the box office this coming weekend as it continues to add screens, and the film already tripled its screen count in Weekend 2. But a long theatrical run and an awards push could realistically get it into the 70s and help it push for the Top 5 among docs.

You can see everything, yes, but even we didn’t necessarily see that one coming.

entry.title: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game
entry.summary: Ray Nicholson and Bill Skarsgård star in an unexceptional sports drama that falls well short of a first down.
entry.content:
There have been any number of movies about the hell of fighting in World War II, the most visceral of which have been made in the years since “Saving Private Ryan” provided a very enduring template for how modern filmmakers could render that carnage with both the spectacle of a blockbuster and the horror of a memory. Peter Berg’s brutal and concussive “The Mosquito Bowl” is definitely one of them! No one could ever say that it’s not.

What differentiates this unsparing epic from the scores of other stories about the Greatest Generation, however, is that some of its characters are good at football. Indeed, these All-American college boys are so good at football that, on Christmas Eve 1944, the soldiers are ordered to play a morale-boosting game of two-hand touch on the beach where their units are preparing for the Battle of Okinawa.

Related Stories
‘The Gilded Age’ Review: Season 4 Is Team Bertha’s Time to Shine
‘I Play Rocky’ Wins Virginia Film Fest Audience Award as Peter Farrelly’s Stallone Drama Readies for Theaters

And for the span of the eight-minute montage during which “The Mosquito Bowl” actually makes good on its title, it’s easy to picture how the famous scrimmage — fought between a roster of impossibly beautiful athletes in their primes — might have been used to backstop a story that accentuated the senseless waste of sending thousands of young men to their deaths. Alas, for the rest of this 126-minute film, that waste is better expressed through Berg’s failure to make anything more of their lives, as the “Spenser Confidential” auteur’s latest Netflix project does almost nothing else to distinguish itself from a genre so well-worn that it’s seemingly run out of ways to blow up a human body.

Why “almost”? I was hoping you wouldn’t ask. For starters, there’s the decision to cast thin-skinned ESPN commentator Pat McAfee as an R. Lee Ermey-inspired drill sergeant. “The Mosquito Bowl” also stands out for how confusingly it conflates the thrill and teamwork of combat sport with the violence and camaraderie of armed conflict; war is presented as both a natural extension of what these boys have been trained to do on the gridiron (to the point that the soldiers briefly diagram their plan of attack as if it were a football play), and also the catastrophe that robbed them of a more innocent purpose. (Berg loves the troops as much as he hates the fact that generals and presidents so wantonly sacrifice their lives.) Someone declares that “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in history,” and yet the film’s characters don’t seem to have any special advantages on the field of battle, as it would be glib to suggest that even the country’s best college running back might be able to slip free of a mortar blast. It’s one thing to argue that football is war, and another, much more asinine thing to argue that war is football.

Perhaps that’s why the Mosquito Bowl itself only took up a single page of the Buzz Bissinger book on which Berg’s film is based, and why that source material used the game as a lens through which a light could be shined on the semi-forgotten men who found their way into the lineup that day. It’s been suggested that Bissinger played up the sports angle in order to capitalize on the success of his “Friday Night Lights,” and given that Berg adapted that book into a film as well, it stands to reason that his “Mosquito Bowl” should do the same.

The problem is that, in stark contrast to Bissinger, Berg and co-writer Mark L. Smith only seem to care about their characters as a means to an end. The project’s anti-war ethos is solely conveyed by reducing collegiate legends into cannon fodder, as the movie is considerably less interested in what bonds these boys together than it is in the shells that blast them apart.

Perhaps that explains why I’ve been able to write almost 650 words without bothering to mention any of their names. To the extent that it matters to a film so blandly de-saturated that everyone in it looks half-dead from the start, Nicholas Galitzine stars as Brown University legend John McLaughry — the only character we know for certain will survive the assault on Japan. (The movie opens with a sustained flash-forward of John staring longingly at an empty football field as “Friday Night Lights” veterans Explosions in the Sky layer their post-rock shimmer over the soundtrack). He’s got sad eyes, a square jaw, and a brunette girlfriend, which is more than you can say for Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), who has a devil-may-care attitude that disappears real quick once his unit makes land on Tawara. The only real source of contextual friction is owed to the rivalry between Purdue fullback Tony Butkovich (a glinty and magnetic Ray Nicholson) and the straight-laced mama’s boy he beat in a big game before the attack on Pearl Harbor (Tom Francis as the stoic and decent Dave Schreiner).

Individually, Butkovich is the only one of these characters who has the chutzpah to carry the movie on his back. Incidentally, he’s the only one of these men who was heading to the pros before the war got in the way. Still, it’s engaging to see them all blitz through life on their home turf, and “The Mosquito Bowl” benefits from Berg’s handheld and ruggedly naturalistic approach to how the players comport themselves off the field (read: they say “fuck” a lot and generally aspire to feel more like real people than they do patronizing impressions of what men were like in the ’40s).

But then the war comes to Hawaii, a match-cut turns a flock of birds into some fighter jets, and these beloved football stars all find themselves rendered nearly anonymous by the sea of shaved heads that are waiting for them at book. Little is made of their civilian celebrity, and even less of their individual decisions to enlist. “This is my rifle — there are many others like it, but this one is mine.”

Berg takes militaristic uniformity as all the excuse he needs to avoid deviating from expectation, and nearly everything that happens between basic training and the big game on the beach near Okinawa feels like it could have happened in several dozen other World War II movies, and almost certainly did. Defiant warriors curdle into terrified kids, bullets whizz through ocean waves, snipers pick off predictable characters at unsuspecting — or very suspecting — moments, and even the most hardened of marines find themselves staring blankly into the middle distance as their friends are decimated on all sides. Berg has always had a flair for the frenetic, and while there’s a perversely fetishistic veneer to the attention he devotes to entrails and enemy screams, it serves the film’s purposes that war has seldom seemed less survivable than it does here. (The film has no interest in humanizing the Japanese, but tries to compensate for that by presenting a few of the Americans as unrepentant monsters).

Still, for all of its supposed verisimilitude, “The Mosquito Bowl” seems less indebted to the reality of war than it does to Hollywood’s idea of it, and its abject refusal to flesh out its characters — a dereliction of duty, if ever there was one — makes it feel more contrived rather than less. I’m happy for Berg that he found a way to combine all of his favorite things into a single project (football, the military, and massive fireballs are all well-accounted for, even if Mark Wahlberg’s absence makes the whole movie feel like it’s forgotten something important), but “The Mosquito Bowl” accomplishes very little beyond violently illustrating that war is worse than football. It does that with such fervor that it loses all sight of what those things might really have in common.

Grade: C

Netflix will release “The Mosquito Bowl” in theaters on Friday, October 30. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, November 25.

entry.title: ‘The Gilded Age’ Review: Season 4 Is Team Bertha’s Time to Shine
entry.summary: 'The Gilded Age' Season 4 focuses on career aspirations and complications, as Carrie Coon's rising socialite, Bertha Russell, ascends to a new plane.
entry.content:
Early in “The Gilded Age” Season 4, during a moment of great tension, a hoity-toity British doctor in a cravat loses his senses and snaps at Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon): “Let me be clear,” the doctor hisses. “You do not understand the situation. Please leave me.”

Bertha, with little more than a flick of her bulging eyes (which could mean anything from “Oh shit” to “If this goes wrong, I will roast your heart over the raging pyre of your dismembered corpse”), does as she’s urged and retreats. The precarious circumstances don’t allow for pushback — time is of the essence — and Bertha, in her boundless wisdom, knows she has no choice but to trust this man and his alleged expertise.

Related Stories
James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next
Why Emmy Wins and Hollywood Recognition Don’t Guarantee Jobs for BIPOC Artists: ‘The Needle Has Not F***ing Moved’

But know this, dear readers: Bertha Russell will not be dismissed again.

Not in Season 4, anyway. Much to the relief of Team Bertha acolytes everywhere (there are dozens of us!), the foreboding events at the end of Season 3 do not elicit further defamation for our masterful social climber. That’s not to say her life is suddenly all sunshine and rainbows. (Although let’s be honest: “The Gilded Age” lives — and thrives — in a world of sunshine and rainbows, where a patient who dies because of segregated hospitals is treated with equal consequence to tea that’s served with too much milk.) (Plus, Bertha’s life in particular is pretty darn close to bliss: hot husband, infinite gowns, gobs of money, a dud of a son, sure, but a boring kid isn’t the worst fate — and Gladys married a duke!)

Nevertheless, amid the relative challenges Bertha faces in Season 4, it’s not a spoiler to report that “The Gilded Age” creator Julian Fellowes and his co-writing executive producer Sonja Warfield wisely refrain from punishing their lovingly nicknamed Opera Mommy for the imaginary crimes cooked up by another man who’s taken leave of his senses: Train Daddy (aka George Russell, aka Morgan Spector, aka the future Robert Langdon). In fact, ol’ George has a pretty rough year—a fitting comeuppance for a once-proud titan of industry who needs to be humbled to remember all he has and who’s to thank for it. (Not to mention a fun season-long arc for Spector, whose growling baritone was begging to break bad anyway.)

Season 3 encouraged a thankless take on Bertha, repeatedly trotting out the idea that her pursuit of power blinded her to the needs of her family: a son who (wrongly) blamed her for his breakup with his vanilla crush, Marian (Louisa Jacobson); a daughter who (briefly) blamed her for an arranged marriage that she soon realized was awesome; and a husband who routinely brings his business to the edge of bankruptcy only to be saved by the brilliant ideas and shrewd scheming of his wife — yet who still somehow thought Bertha was the one playing it too fast and loose with their family’s love.

Bertha, after all, is only guilty of doing what’s best for her daughter, raising her family’s clout, and preserving the Russell name as essential benefactors of the arts (that new opera house didn’t open itself) rather than greedy railroad tycoons with terminal severance packages. Suggesting anything else was, to be frank, imbecilic, but “The Gilded Age” played it out through the final shot, where a distraught Bertha watched her jealous husband ride off in a huff after informing her he wouldn’t be coming home until he “knows what he wants.”

That’s where Season 4 picks up: months later, but the mood unchanged. Bertha is on the other side of the ocean, caring for a very pregnant Gladys (Taissa Farmiga), while George is in the States, struggling to keep his business in the black. Elsewhere in New York, Peggy (Denée Benton) savors the success of her first novel while her fiancé, the nice doctor William (Jordan Donica), moves up in the medical ranks. Jack (Ben Ahlers) is getting comfortable in his new house, courtesy of his innovative alarm clocks, but he’s less comfortable with his new status (which requires etiquette classes from his servant friends) and his next invention (which isn’t as easy to sell as the first).

Everyone is moving up! Building careers! Making names for themselves! And then there’s Larry (Harry Richardson) and Marian, who bounce between tedious flirtations and equally tedious frustrations, almost like they’re two attractive twenty-somethings who desperately want to bone but can only get there by boring the pants off each other. Admittedly, Marian gestures toward finding a purpose beyond playing house by volunteering to help the less fortunate, but even Elizabeth Marvel, the program’s guiding hand, struggles to keep our aspiring housewife from dreaming of her sole, snoozy passion.

Luckily, Agnes (Christine Baranski) and Ada (Cynthia Nixon) are more than happy to spice things up: The latter falls for forbidden fruit, and the former hosts the President of the United States.

You read that right: the President of America agrees to have dinner at Agnes’ cozy Manhattan mansion, which provides the seasonal centerpiece “Gilded Age” fans are sure to be sick over: Who’s invited? What will be served? What will they wear? All these gossipy questions and more help structure the better part of Season 4, building ample anticipation for the historic evening by pitting as many of its invited guests against each other as possible in a steel-cage death match of affronted expressions and polite self-satisfaction.

The stakes are set as finely as the silverware, with bragging rights — for socialites and their servers — taking dramatic precedence over the fate of American rail travel, as it should be: In “The Gilded Age,” who saves face is always more substantial than whatever unnamed sums are secured or squandered, and the presence of POTUS does little to upend those pleasingly backward priorities.

Speaking of presence, Season 4 does feel the squeeze of its sprawling cast. It’s a little too light on downstairs character development, even if the dinner involves a few favorites and implements one outstanding plot device I shan’t spoil here. Some supporting players go underutilized (Jack as well as the scheming, wannabe power couple, Oscar and Enid), while unworthy regulars become story anchors entrusted with too much emotional weight. (By now, you surely know to whom I’m referring.)

Ah, so it goes in a series with an insatiable appetite for perpetual opulence and little tolerance for legitimate loss. Far be it from me to say what influences Fellowes, but he seems unwilling to repeat past mistakes or kill off a beloved character — any beloved character — too soon, if at all.

And that’s just fine. Really! We need more cheery, soapy TV filled with simple delights. “The Gilded Age” is the rare HBO Sunday-night staple with even-keeled ambitions and no extra-dour drama. It’s a frothy, let’s-leave-’em-smiling show that’s open to acknowledging serious issues — misogyny, bigotry, and oppression all inform the cast’s choices, to one extent or another — so long as they don’t linger long enough to spoil the vibe.

That’s why Bertha’s ascendance comes as such a relief. Nothing ruins a good time like misplaced sympathy, and siding with the man of the house in a series that’s more rooted in women’s perspectives with each passing season just feels wrong. What little deep thinking “The Gilded Age” invites, there’s something to be said for how it depicts women shaping a country that actively tries to operate outside of their reach. Bertha, with her new money and never-say-die demeanor, isn’t afraid to roll up her sleeves and do whatever it takes. Seeing her shine isn’t just good and right given her specific circumstances (re: George); it’s good and right because it bucks historical precedent (rah-rah, feminism!).

She grasps each situation perfectly — and she’s not going anywhere. Thank goodness.

Grade: B

“The Gilded Age” Season 4 premieres Sunday, November 1 at 9 p.m. ET on HBO. New episodes will be released weekly through the finale on December 20.

entry.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Wins Virginia Film Fest Audience Award as Peter Farrelly’s Stallone Drama Readies for Theaters
entry.summary: The 39th Virginia Film Festival audience awards were led by Peter Farrelly's 'I Play Rocky.' See the full winners list.
entry.content:
IndieWire just returned from the Virginia Film Festival in charming Charlottesville, which drew a smattering of starry attendees and showcased awards-season favorites on the big screen. Below, we announce this year’s audience award winners, led by Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky” in the narrative feature category.

Celebrating the festival’s 39th year, executive director Jody Kielbasa and artistic director Ilya Tovbis and their teams drew in more than 26,600 attendees, with 134 features screened Wednesday through Sunday, and more than 120 industry guests.

Matthew Syrett and Bowie Alexander’s nonfiction “Admission Possible” won the documentary feature audience award. The acquisition title follows seven first-generation high-schoolers in New York City as they work to secure a future for their families and themselves.

Related Stories
Gotham Film Awards 2026 Nominations Spread the Love from ‘All of a Sudden’ to ‘The Invite’
Luchino Visconti’s Tragic, Beautiful Final Film ‘L’Innocente’ Restored in 4K — Watch the Trailer

Teddy Stern’s narrative short “Getar Hero,” about a cowboy living in Bombay, won that audience prize, while the documentary short “Sarah Ann Kelley: Becoming Visible” also resonated with audiences. It centers on an 85-year-old Charlottesville native who broke racial and gender boundaries.

Amazon MGM’s “I Play Rocky” was the first runner-up for the Toronto International Film Festival People’s Choice Award this year, behind Netflix’s “La Bola Negra.” The Oscar race appears to be a showdown between “La Bola Negra” and Universal’s “The Odyssey” right now, but don’t underestimate “I Play Rocky’s” appeal to crack the Best Picture 10.

Anthony Ippolito gives a star-making performance as Sylvester Stallone, who writes and stars in 1977’s Oscar Best Picture winner, “Rocky,” after eager producers Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff court him to snap up his first script. Sly, meanwhile, fights to also play the lead, which he eventually does as “I Play Rocky” recreates the film‘s scrappy production. Tracy Letts steals the movie as a dryly observant United Artists studio head who’s eventually disarmed by Sly’s charms. Last week, I sat for an intimate media screening of “I Play Rocky” that played all the way to the back of the room, with even an audience that small audibly cheering for the movie. It opens in select theaters November 6 ahead of a November 20 Thanksgiving-adjacent wide release. The film isn’t universally beloved by critics, though.

Virginia Film Festival‘s lineup included films like opener “The Debut,” international Oscar hopefuls “Rose,” “All of a Sudden,” and “Minotaur,” and deserving indies like Gotham-nominated “Mouse,” all of which played well to local audiences. IndieWire hosted a live “Screen Talk” podcast with “Paper Tiger” director James Gray ahead of his film’s celebrated premiere in Virginia (we’ll debut it next week on podcast platforms). Jessica Lange and Nathan Lange were among the top-tier talent who also gave live talks. David O. Russell, meanwhile, and producer Todd Black showed first-look footage of his NFL biopic “Madden,” starring Nicolas Cage in heavy prosthetics.

Virginia Film Festival Audience Awards are listed below. The festival is a program of the University of Virginia, which boasts a sprawlingly beautiful campus not far from the Downtown Mall district that hosts the festival screenings.

Narrative Feature: “I Play Rocky”
Documentary Feature: “Admission Possible”
Narrative Short: “Getar Hero”
Documentary Short: “Sarah Ann Kelley: Becoming Visible”

entry.title: Gotham Film Awards 2026 Nominations Spread the Love from ‘All of a Sudden’ to ‘The Invite’
entry.summary: See the full list of 2026 Gotham Film Awards nominations, led by 'All of a Sudden,' 'The Invite,' 'Tender Loving Care,' and more.
entry.content:
The 2026 Gotham Film Awards nominations are in, setting the stage for the next phase of the movie awards season. While last year’s nominations and wins were topped by “One Battle After Another,” which went on to win the Best Picture Oscar, the organization decided to show some “Tender Loving Care” to more films this time around. The new Mike Leigh film is among five nomination leaders this year, along with “All of a Sudden,” “Clarissa,” “La Gradiva,” and “The Invite.” Each scored four nominations.

The 2026 nominations also mark the return of the Gotham Audience Award after a six-year hiatus. The honor celebrates films that transcend the screen to become defining cultural moments, capturing audiences’ attention through their impact, reach, and resonance. Gotham members will vote to determine the winner, and the award will be presented to the film’s credited director(s) and producer(s). (In short, the prize indexes a film’s popularity in culture through audience response and box office.)

Related Stories
Watch ‘My Undesirable Friends’ Director Julia Loktev Recall the Week Russia Invaded Ukraine
‘Wildwood’ Sparked a Much-Needed Comeback for Laika at the Box Office

This year, the Gotham Audience Award nominees were curated from films submitted to The Gothams for consideration, measured by opening-weekend per-theater average against the highest-rated and most-watched films of 2026, as reported in box office tracking and on Letterboxd. Notable films not submitted for any Gotham Awards consideration include “The Odyssey” and “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

“It’s a pleasure to announce this year’s nominees. It has been a remarkable year for film, with audiences turning out in theaters for bold, distinctive work from first-time filmmakers and established artists alike,” said Jeffrey Sharp, Gotham Film & Media Institute executive director. “This year’s nominations, alongside our Tributes and the return of the Audience Award, reflect that abundance and celebrate the creative community that has been at the heart of The Gothams for more than three decades.”

While the Gotham nominations committees are made up of clusters of critics, filmmakers, and tastemakers (including IndieWire Editorial Director Kate Erbland and Chief Film Critic David Ehrlich), rather than an 11,000-member Academy, these awards often help put less publicized films onto Oscar voters’ radars. Example: Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson’s extraordinary “Mouse” in the Best Feature category, which premiered way back at the Berlin Film Festival and is primed for an awards-season relaunch.

entry.title: Luchino Visconti’s Tragic, Beautiful Final Film ‘L’Innocente’ Restored in 4K — Watch the Trailer
entry.summary: Watch the trailer for the 4K restoration of Italian master filmmaker Luchino Visconti's marital melodrama 'L'Innocente' from 1976.
entry.content:
Luchino Visconti‘s lush, aristocratic worlds have seen a major revival at repertory movie houses over the past year. From the black-and-white “White Nights” with Marcello Mastroianni to the psychosexual queer drama “Conversation Piece” with Burt Lancaster, the Italian grandmaster’s vivid melodramas capture souls adrift, possessive, and tragic. While Visconti is probably best known for epics like “The Leopard” and “Rocco and His Brothers,” in his later career up until his death in 1976, the Palme d’Or-winning filmmaker turned his lens on more intimate dramas and marital discord.

A new restoration of Visconti’s final film, “L’Innocente,” premiered in Cannes Classics and at the New York Film Festival. Starring Giancarlo Giannini, Laura Antonelli, and Jennifer O’Neill, the film was lovingly restored by Film Movement Classics to preserve the film’s 50th anniversary. Below, IndieWire debuts the exclusive trailer for the new release. A theatrical rollout begins December 11.

Related Stories
Watch ‘My Undesirable Friends’ Director Julia Loktev Recall the Week Russia Invaded Ukraine
‘Wildwood’ Sparked a Much-Needed Comeback for Laika at the Box Office

Set in Rome at the turn of the 20th century, the film centers on “a wealthy and self-absorbed nobleman Tullio Hermil (Giancarlo Giannini) [who] carries on an affair with a sophisticated yet possessive widow, Countess Teresa Raffo (Jennifer O’Neill), while treating his devoted wife, Giuliana (Laura Antonelli), with cold condescension. Wounded by his years of neglect, Giuliana takes a lover of her own with young novelist, Filippo (Marc Porel). When she becomes pregnant with Filippo’s child, Tullio’s wounded pride cannot be contained, setting off a chain of events leading to ultimate tragedy.”

The film loosely adapts Gabriele D’Annunzio’s 1892 novel. At the time of production, Visconti had suffered a major stroke a few years prior that didn’t necessarily impact his ability to work, but it made him a liability in terms of securing casting. For “L’Innocente,” Visconti had wanted his “The Leopard” and “Rocco and His Brothers” star, the French actor Alain Delon, in the lead. He also wanted Delon’s ex and repeat Visconti star Romy Schneider in the film, too, as well as Charlotte Rampling (“The Damned”) at one point. Visconti died in March 1976, just two months ahead of the film’s Cannes premiere. Critic Jonathan Rosenbaum called the film “a withering autocritique of masculine vanity and self-delusion.”

Cinelab Service in Italy created a new 4K digital transfer on an Arriscan film scanner, working from the original camera negative.

entry.title: How Two Rival Columnists Created Hollywood’s Gossip Machine — and Taught America to Worship Attention
entry.summary: An excerpt from Eileen Cope's 'Hollywood Whispers: The Untold Story of the Original Gossip Queens, Louella Parsons and Hedda Hopper' charts their rise
entry.content:
In her new book, “Hollywood Whispers: The Untold Story of the Original Gossip Queens, Louella Parsons and Hedda Hopper,” Eileen Cope delves into a rivalry that dramatically shaped the entertainment industry and culture at large throughout the mid-20th century. After the birth of the star system in Hollywood, Parsons and Hopper rose to prominence as gossip columnists who could make and break careers, and choose to keep or expose celebrities’ secrets. With a combined readership of 75 million at their peak, Hopper and Parsons wielded extraordinary influence — and instilled paralyzing fear. As columnist Liz Smith has written, “The studios created both of them. And they thought they could control both of them. But they became Frankenstein monsters escaped from the labs.” In the excerpt below, Cope summarizes their stark differences — and even more striking similarities.

Related Stories
What the Success of ’28 Weeks Later’ Meant for an ‘Indiewood’ Still Finding Its Footing
What’s It Like to Be a Hair and Fur Fabricator for Laika? A New Book Will Answer That (and More)

Hollywood has always been a hall of mirrors. What began as an industry of light and illusion had, by the 1940s, become a machinery of control—an empire built on fantasy, running on fear. Its dreammakers no longer needed scripts or cameras to keep order. They had Louella Parsons and Hedda Hopper.

By then, both women had transcended the ordinary limits of journalism. They were not simply reporters; they were gatekeepers of belief, the quiet regulators of a nation’s imagination. To cross them was to risk vanishing—not merely from the screen, but from the collective story America told about itself.

Hollywood insiders referred to them—half jokingly, half in dread—as “the High Priestesses.” Studio secretaries clipped their columns before the morning dailies reached the lot, marking any mention of the studio’s stars with red pencil. Publicists phoned assistants in panic if a name appeared in the wrong context. “They could wreck you before lunch,” remembered producer Pandro Berman. “And by dinner, they’d make you again—if it suited them.”

It was easy, at first, to mistake their power for personality. Louella, with her sanctimonious charm and the backing of William Randolph Hearst, ruled the studios from her desk at the Los Angeles Examiner. Her typewriter was a throne. Her column ran like clockwork through America’s breakfast tables, a sermon of what was right and who had sinned. Hedda, the actress-turned-crusader, cultivated a different tone—brassy, righteous, vengeful. Her voice carried across radio waves like a call to arms. She didn’t just write gossip; she announced it, her cadence turning every name into an accusation or an absolution.

Both women understood theater. Louella played the role of moral mother, her column written in the soothing cadences of propriety—rarely venomous on the surface, yet devastating in its implications. Hedda was the showwoman. “When she walked into Ciro’s,” recalled gossip photographer Frank Worth, “it was like someone had switched on the lights.” Even those who loathed her found themselves glancing up, afraid she might be looking at them.

Louella and Hedda were two sides of the same coin, minted in a culture that worshipped celebrity and feared moral chaos. Each understood what the studios feared most: scandal, exposure, the sudden rupture of the illusion. And they learned to trade in that fear, turning rumor into regulation.

Louella had built her empire first. By the early 1930s, her column appeared in hundreds of newspapers through the Hearst syndicate, reaching an estimated twenty million readers daily. Hollywood Hotel, her weekly radio show, brought the glamour of opening nights directly into American living rooms. Its mix of studio orchestras, star appearances, and previews of upcoming films created a powerful cycle of cross-promotion: her print column drove listeners to the broadcast, and the broadcast reinforced her authority in print.

She was feared as much as courted. Stars who crossed her found themselves frozen out. Studio executives who annoyed her might find their films receiving tepid coverage. A single line hinting that an actor appeared “unhappy with recent assignments” could trigger studio meetings and contract reviews. Louella’s prose was brief, polite, and devastatingly coded; her readers learned to interpret her tone as carefully as her text. The fear she inspired was not only of what she printed but of what she might choose not to.

The competition she could not have predicted came in the form of a woman she had once treated as a harmless curiosity. By 1935, Hedda Hopper’s film career was essentially over. She was fifty, though she claimed forty-five, watching her savings evaporate and terrified about her future. When a studio executive suggested she could “transition to extra work,” Hedda turned the humiliation into fuel. If she couldn’t star in movies, she would make herself the story. The weapon she would wield was not beauty or youth, but the pen.

When a friend suggested she try writing a gossip column, Hedda was insulted. Writing gossip seemed like a public acknowledgment that she couldn’t make it as a performer. But desperation has a way of making humiliation seem acceptable. She borrowed a typewriter, set up at her kitchen table, and began by writing what she knew best: the petty rivalries of actors who had underestimated her. “I never lied,” she said later, “but I didn’t always tell the truth either.” The early columns were messy but alive, full of energy and vengeance.

Then Hedda got angry. She stopped trying to write like a journalist and started writing like herself— sharp, critical, unsparing, willing to say things other columnists wouldn’t dare print. Twenty years as a working actress had also given her something valuable: relationships with the people Louella ignored. Character actors, crew members, hairdressers, chauffeurs, and wardrobe girls had no loyalty to Louella, and many were happy to talk to Hedda, who had once been one of them.

The Los Angeles Times noticed. Hearst’s primary competitor in Southern California saw Hedda as a weapon against his dominance through Louella. In 1938, the paper offered Hedda a contract with better pay, more resources, and a much larger platform. She would compete directly with the woman who had been Hollywood’s undisputed gossip queen for fifteen years.

Most people thought she would be crushed. Instead, Hedda transformed herself for the opportunity. She began wearing the enormous hats that became her trademark—creations decorated with feathers, flowers, fruit, and even stuffed animals. The hats ensured that everyone at a Hollywood event knew when Hedda Hopper had arrived. She also developed a confrontational style that contrasted with Louella’s cozy approach. Where Louella praised, Hedda criticized. Where Louella protected relationships, Hedda burned bridges. Where Louella sought to be loved, Hedda was content to be feared.

In the beginning, the difference between them seemed simple enough. Louella had the empire; Hedda had the instinct. Louella’s authority came from her link to Hearst—a patriarchal structure she both served and mastered. Hedda’s came from sheer velocity. She moved fast, wrote fast, spoke fast. She had learned that outrage was more contagious than affection.

At first, the two women coexisted uneasily, even politely. Louella sent Hedda a congratulatory telegram when her first radio broadcast went national. Hedda responded with a bouquet of orchids and a note that read, “To the Queen of the Kingdom I am only visiting.” But the civility evaporated as soon as Hedda’s column began pulling readers away from the Examiner. In 1940, when Hedda’s column syndication reached more than six million households, Louella persuaded Hearst’s editors to bar her rival from every Hearst-owned paper.

As the 1940s unfolded, their feud became public theater. Columns answered columns. Louella hinted that Hedda was “overly dramatic.” Hedda fired back, calling Louella “a relic of studio servitude.” Studios courted both women, sometimes feeding them different versions of the same story to see who would publish first. Readers began to choose sides.

In 1945, Photoplay published “Battle of the Typewriters,” complete with caricatures of the two women as dueling queens—Louella seated on a gilt throne, Hedda brandishing her hatpins like weapons. The story outsold every issue that year except the one featuring Clark Gable’s return from the war. The public couldn’t get enough. For a nation recovering from global conflict, the spectacle of two powerful women waging a cold war of words was irresistible.

Their methods echo through the media that followed. The tabloid boom of the 1980s, TMZ, Instagram, celebrity influencers, blind-item accounts, and the daily social-media outrage cycle all trace their lineage to the template Louella and Hedda built. They understood that access could be traded, intimacy manufactured, morality weaponized, and a public image constructed or destroyed through repetition. The machine they built continues to hum behind every red carpet and every scandal recycled for entertainment. What they truly enshrined was attention—and America never stopped worshiping it.

The women themselves could not stop Hollywood from moving on. As the studio system declined and stars emerged, the two gossip queens became relics of the world they had once governed. When the Los Angeles Examiner folded in 1962, Louella suffered a professional blow. Already showing signs of physical deterioration, she nevertheless continued going out, bejeweled and bewildered, like a dowager empress whose country had overthrown her rule. She finally retired in 1965, beset by further medical problems.

Hedda had always advised leaving a party before the glow faded. On February 1, 1966, she died in Los Angeles of double pneumonia at the age of eighty. Her cryptic parting words were entirely in character: “They should know what I haven’t written!”

Louella’s daughter, Harriet, visited her mother at the Santa Monica nursing home to deliver the news that Hedda Hopper was dead. Louella sat in profound silence, then appeared confused. She would live for another six years, largely withdrawn from the world she had once ruled, before dying of arteriosclerosis on December 9, 1972, at the age of ninety-one. But on hearing that her great rival had finally departed, Louella gathered herself long enough to offer one last, unmistakable verdict: “GOOD!”

Adapted from “Hollywood Whispers: The Untold Story of the Original Gossip Queens, Louella Parsons and Hedda Hopper” available November 3 from Lyons Press.

entry.title: Watch ‘My Undesirable Friends’ Director Julia Loktev Recall the Week Russia Invaded Ukraine
entry.summary: Watch 'My Undesirable Friends' director Julia Loktev's appearance at IndieWire's Art of the Doc.
entry.content:
Great documentaries never turn out quite the way you plan them. You might start out thinking that you’re making one film, but a documentarian has to be willing to accept when changes in the lives of their subjects changes the nature of their project.

Julia Loktev‘s two-part documentary “My Undesirable Friends” is a perfect example of this. The films, which follow journalists at TV Rain, which was Russia’s last independent news channel before it was shut down over coverage of the war in Ukraine, began as a story about journalists working in a hostile climate. But when her subjects were forced to flee the country and scatter across Europe, “My Undesirable Friends” had to expand its scale.

Related Stories
‘Wildwood’ Sparked a Much-Needed Comeback for Laika at the Box Office
James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next

During a conversation with IndieWire’s Chris O’Falt at our Art of the Doc event, Loktev opened up about the project’s origins. While she had already been shooting footage of her subjects, the films truly took shape the week Russia invaded Ukraine.

“Neither of these two films were supposed to happen,” Loktev said. “I just started making a film that I thought was gonna be called ‘The Lives of Foreign Agents’ about these young journalists that were being called foreign agents. And the media were being called undesirable organizations. Of course, what we didn’t know was that four and a half months later, Russia would start a full scale war with Ukraine and shut down all independent media within that first week.”

“‘Part II’ starts right after all these journalists were forced to leave the country,” she continued. “Putin calls them the flies that Russia spits out of its mouth. But that first week was terrifying. Nobody could imagine invading Ukraine. The war had been going for eight years, but it was the kind of year where the world allowed Russia to host a world cup… All of these journalists tried to report the truth to Russians, and up until that moment they were living in Russia. Maybe you were waiting for the police to show up at your office or your home, maybe friends of yours were being arrested, but you could still work in Russia. And then that stopped.”

Watch the complete conversation with Loktev in the video above.
