Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com, or find us on Facebook,Twitter,Instagram, and YouTube.

entry.title: ‘Wildwood’ Sparked a Much-Needed Comeback for Laika at the Box Office
entry.summary: 'Wildwood,' Laika's latest stop-motion animated epic, made $12.2 million domestic at the box office, on par with some of its past hits.
entry.content:
The release of Laika‘s “Wildwood” at the box office this weekend was about more than just the dollars and cents or the success or failure of a single film; in some ways it was about the future of a fan-favorite film studio.

“Wildwood” is the Portland, Oregon-based stop-motion animation studio’s sixth animated feature but also the first movie released by the studio in seven years. Easily director Travis Knight’s most ambitious project to date under the Laika banner, it’s been in the works for even longer than that time gap: fans have been awaiting it for years. Heck, we’ve been talking about this movie since last year.

What Laika needed with “Wildwood” was not just a solid number but a display of genuine enthusiasm that this movie could reintroduce audiences to the studio. Even if a movie like “Coraline,” Laika’s debut, breakout stop-motion hit, was not a gangbusters blockbuster upon its release, it’s a film that has had real staying power and made a legacy for Laika in the process.

Related Stories
James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next
Laika and Fathom Take Legal Action to Stop ‘Wildwood’ Screenings at L.A.’s Bruin Theatre

“Wildwood” grossed $12.2 million domestic in its opening weekend, placing it at No. 3 for the weekend behind “Clayface” and “You Can See Everything. It also added an additional $2.9 million from a handful of international markets and still has a lot to go. Those aren’t eye-popping numbers, and when you hear reports that the budget is around $100 million, it’s not a surprise that many of the headlines surrounding “Wildwood” are that it could be a big money loser.

But having expensive, hand-crafted passion projects that view budgets as an after-thought are kind of part of Laika’s DNA. And it’s clear after one weekend that “Wildwood” is not the let down its previous feature, 2019’s “Missing Link,” turned out to be. That film opened to less than half of what “Wildwood” did with just $5.9 million and finished at $17 million domestic, a number “Wildwood” will easily surpass.

The better comp for “Wildwood” is “Kubo and the Two Strings,” which opened to $12.6 million and finished with $48 million domestic and $76 million worldwide. It’s also not far off from DreamWorks’ “Forgotten Island” from earlier this year, which opened to $13 million and has made $67.9 million worldwide thus far.

The key though is for “Wildwood” to repeat the stellar holds and word of mouth over time that some of its past hits have done. All five of its previous films have had hefty multiples, including “Coraline” (4.5x), “ParaNorman” (4.1x), and “Kubo and the Two Strings” (3.8x). A 3.8 multiple for “Wildwood,” same as “Kubo,” would have it finish with roughly $46.3 million domestic.

Some of the early exit tracking suggests it has a chance to be even better than that. “Wildwood” received an A CinemaScore and almost universal positive scores and “recommend” grades from PostTrak, in addition to a 99 percent on Rotten Tomatoes at time of writing. It had strong per-screen-averages across 395 PLFs and some Dolby Cinemas in particular, and it even packed houses in places like Portland where the film is set and pays homage.

Dave Burke, Laika’s Chief Marketing Officer and an EP on the film, told IndieWire those figures suggest it could even add a few screens beyond the 2,940 it had this first weekend. Alamo Drafthouse for one played the film on 11 screens and is looking to add another six, Burke said. Also of note is that this is one of Fathom Entertainment’s first truly wide releases for an original film after having big success re-releasing “Coraline,” so both companies are viewing these numbers as encouraging.

“I think we needed to prove ourselves as the new kid on the block, and I think the data points to the fact that there’s a really compelling business case for exhibition to get on even more robustly and support the film in the kind of coming weeks,” Burke said.

Many of Laika’s films have been darker in nature, and “Wildwood” does not shy away from that. The studio has been upfront in its marketing that the film is PG-13, that it aims to reach a general audience rather than kids, and is based on a middlegrade novel from Colin Meloy, better known as the lead singer of the indie folk band The Decemberists. It’s an intense and often violent display of puppetry with a third act that resembles a “Lord of the Rings” war sequence. But even so Burke said the film had a strong showing from the under 34 crowd and a good mix of tweens coming along with their parents. It even received a 5-star grade from the parents’ guide Common Sense Media. These are the types of fans Laika needs to cultivate to get them to revisit their older titles and keep them excited as the company is set to expand into live-action films and whatever other passion project Travis Knight has cooking next.

“People have just really recognized from the get go this is an extraordinary undertaking, and there’s been a real sense that everyone is willing for us to succeed, and I think that is something that we don’t take lightly,” Burke said. “We have a responsibility to make sure that this film gets seen by the widest possible audience, and that’s why I’m so focused on the next couple of weeks, but also its afterlife and what its legacy looks like.”

entry.title: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next
entry.summary: After 'Superman,' 'Supergirl,' 'Lanterns,' and 'Clayface,' how is the James Gunn/Peter Safran DC Studios experiment going?
entry.content:
Four years ago this week, James Gunn and Peter Safran were handed one of Hollywood’s most coveted, and impossible, jobs. When they were named co-CEOs of Warner Bros.’ DC Studios label, they received complete oversight of comic book characters like Superman, Wonder Woman, Batman* (more on that later), Green Lantern, the Flash, and countless others. With a seemingly blank canvas to make as many movies and shows as their hearts desired, the implied mandate was clear: get DC Comics out of second place.

The studio’s DC division spent much of the 2010s as a laughingstock while its Marvel competitors seemed to never miss. Despite having a better roster of characters — 20 years ago, mentioning the Guardians of the Galaxy in the same breath as Batman would have been laughable even to the biggest comic book nerd — Warner Bros. couldn’t figure out how to turn its characters into must-see cinema. The incredible cultural moment of the Christopher Nolan Batman movies gave way to one misfire after another: Zack Snyder’s “Man of Steel” gave way to the “Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice” debacle, Patty Jenkins’ acclaimed “Wonder Woman” movie led to a critically panned sequel, and the studio’s attempt to launch its own “Avengers” with “Justice League” was bad enough to leave fans arguing about different cuts instead of wondering where the story went next.

Related Stories
Laika and Fathom Take Legal Action to Stop ‘Wildwood’ Screenings at L.A.’s Bruin Theatre
‘Elastic Hearts’ Filmmakers Claim Their Movie Was Denied a Texas Tax Incentive Over Abortion Storyline

It was the kind of turnaround project that entitles its leaders to a long runway. After Gunn and Safran accepted the job in late 2022, they began announcing projects in early 2023. Then they had to shoot and edit them, meaning that we didn’t really see the vision take shape until this year. But now we’ve seen Gunn and Safran release three major theatrical films, two live-action shows, and multiple animated ones — more than enough of a sample size to start grading their creative direction. Even if we’re still in Phase One of their long-term plan, the pros and cons of their studio approach are becoming clear.

The Films

Gunn and Safran kicked off their DC tenure with the safest and smartest film they could have possibly made: a “Superman” movie written and directed by Gunn himself. Putting DC’s signature character in the hands of a filmmaker with an unimpeachable ability to deliver smart popcorn fare was a no-brainer. And in many ways, “Superman” delivered.

The film wisely skipped the obligatory origin story that everyone already knows, checking in with the man formerly known as Kal-El after he had already assumed his dual role of Superman and Clark Kent on Earth. Gunn brought his signature blend of heart, humor, and needle drops, delivering an entertaining blockbuster that stood in clear contrast to the excessively dark DC films of the 2010s. This movie was colorful and fun, even in its heaviest moments. Unsurprisingly, it grossed over $600 million worldwide — though it still didn’t tell us much about Gunn’s ability to run a studio. His bona fides as a comic book writer/director were never in doubt, but we still hadn’t seen him supervise other filmmakers.

Those opportunities came in 2026, and the results were more polarizing. The studio’s second film, “Supergirl,” was one of the year’s most public flops. Milly Alcock’s eponymous character appeared briefly in “Superman,” but Craig Gillespie’s film traded its predecessor’s grounded Earth drama for a space western set across a series of “Mad Max”-esque planets. The confusing mythology and grating visual effects felt like a departure, and the film received mixed reviews and only made $100 million worldwide despite costing nearly twice that. Equally concerning were reports about creative clashes between Gunn and Safran and Gillespie, with two competing cuts being screened against each other months before the movie opened.

Then came “Clayface.” James Watkins’ origin story for an obscure Batman villain was branded as a horror movie that just happened to exist within a comic book universe. The gory, goopy story of an actor who sacrifices everything to regain his skin-deep beauty wasn’t for everyone, but it represented a real creative swing. And it was made on a responsible $44 million budget, which removed the pressure to be universally appealing.

It’s easy to see a world where this DC universe thrives with a combination of major tentpoles directed by Gunn (who is already hard at work on a “Superman” follow-up dated for July 2027) and smaller, weirder films based on minor characters. But we still haven’t seen Gunn and Safran oversee a blockbuster that connects with mainstream audiences with another filmmaker in the director’s chair. “Supergirl” may end up being an anomaly, but right now it still represents one-third of their theatrical output. That sadly has to count for something.

Grade: B–

The Shows

Gunn and Safran’s overhaul of DC’s TV output technically began before they took over as CEOs, as “Peacemaker” premiered on HBO Max nine months earlier. Created (and largely directed) by Gunn, the raunchy action comedy saw John Cena reprising his role from Gunn’s “Suicide Squad” movie as an antihero willing to kill as many men, women, and children as he needs to achieve his goal of world peace. Gunn’s sensibilities were still there, but the HBO brand let the show include far more nudity and profanity than you’d ever find in a four-quadrant film. A hit with fans and critics, “Peacemaker” reminded audiences what was possible when you had access to a premium cable brand to complement your theatrical films.

Their first official project after taking the reins was also a TV show. The animated “Creature Commandos” debuted on HBO Max in December 2024 with an inoffensive six-episode Season 1 that showcased Gunn’s favorite themes about weirdos who assemble their own found families. The business stakes were low — fairly or not, the average consumer isn’t watching animated superhero shows, and the diehard fans who do tune in are unlikely to ever stop supporting DC’s other projects. But the series has one notable wrinkle: Gunn cast its voice actors with the intention of reprising their roles in live-action projects, a tactic he says he plans to use on all future animated projects.

“Peacemaker” also concluded with a well-received Season 2, but the real test of the DC Universe’s TV output came this fall with “Lanterns.” Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof, and Tom King’s series about DC’s intergalactic police force more than delivered on its promise to be “True Detective” with Green Lanterns. The film uses classic police procedural tropes — the show centers on an older, set-in-his-ways Green Lantern who reluctantly partners with a talented young partner he won’t give the time of day to — in a dark, season-long murder saga set in middle America. The show itself received rave reviews, but its actual contents matter less than what it represents: a unique, auteur-driven project that fits into Gunn and Safran’s storyline while allowing other filmmakers to showcase their own voices. So far, it’s the ultimate example of what the CEOs have always said they wanted their DC Studios to do.

Grade: A-

The Batman Problem

Perhaps the biggest variable facing Gunn and Safran’s DC Studios is largely outside their control. Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” had already opened in theaters a few months before they took over, and Warner Bros. announced that the Robert Pattinson-led series would continue separately from the new DC Universe. A second film is in production, with Steven Soderbergh helping to complete principal photography, and HBO shows like “The Penguin” and the recently announced “Poison Ivy” continue to expand the mythology.

Gunn and Safran have some involvement in these “Batman” projects and publicly support them, but the films and shows exist outside the overarching storyline they’re trying to build. And while it’s not an insurmountable problem — multiple artists working with the same characters in different timelines has been a trademark of comic books from the very beginning — it’s also not ideal to have one of your franchise’s two biggest characters tied up outside your purview.

Nothing’s stopping Gunn and Safran from bringing in their own Batman, and it seems inevitable that it will happen soon. “Clayface” takes place in Gotham City, and once you start introducing Batman villains, you need to give audiences something to fight them. Gunn and Safran previously tapped Andy Muschietti to direct a Batman movie called “The Brave and the Bold,” which was still in development as of 2025, but no cast or release date has been announced.

Many fans and Warner Bros. shareholders believe this DC Universe won’t reach its full potential until it introduces its own Batman. The kind of major team-up movies with billion-dollar box office potential, like a new “Justice League” or a “World’s Finest” team-up between Batman and Superman, all feature the Dark Knight. And assuming their Batman isn’t Robert Pattinson, they’ll inevitably be faced with audiences who wonder why or see theirs as a second-tier product.

It’s not fair to grade Gunn and Safran on this problem, since they didn’t create it, but they still have to navigate it. Again, it’s not insurmountable, but Kevin Feige never had to deal with this at Marvel.

Grade: N/A

The Process

Gunn and Safran’s overarching DC story is still in its infancy, but their development process has become clear. And it’s arguably their best asset. In many ways, their DC Studios can be described as the anti-MCU. Whereas their competitor (and Gunn’s former employer) became famous for seeing everything as part of a larger puzzle, DC Studios seems much more focused on treating each film as a standalone project. Films are greenlit based on the quality of their individual scripts, not the Easter eggs that connect them. Nobody would ever tell you that a brand-new DC cinematic universe should release “Clayface” as one of its first films, but Gunn has openly said Mike Flanagan’s script stood out among the many other projects they were developing. The script was ready; therefore, they made the movie.

Prioritizing scripts over corporate synergy should be music to the ears of cinephiles burned out on Marvel’s assembly-line approach to storytelling. That means continuity will never be as tight as what you find in the MCU, and plenty of projects will be announced without ever coming to fruition. (We’re still upset about James Mangold’s “Swamp Thing” and Luca Guadagnino’s “Sgt. Rock” falling through the cracks, but it’s better than rushing out movies that aren’t ready.) Comic book fans used to following these companies like sports teams might need to adjust their expectations, but movie lovers who care less about those details should get richer viewing experiences. It’s also better for the creatives who get a chance to pitch their own original ideas and put their own stamp on beloved characters.

The only thing holding this back from an “A” grade is the fact that ideals that sound good on paper still have to be executed. I deeply admire Gunn for publicly declaring that no DC Studios movie will receive a release date until everyone is happy with the script. But I also saw “Supergirl” and wondered what this mysterious great script could have possibly looked like, and why it apparently didn’t make it into the finished movie.

Grade: B+

entry.title: Laika and Fathom Take Legal Action to Stop ‘Wildwood’ Screenings at L.A.’s Bruin Theatre
entry.summary: Laika and Fathom tell IndieWire they're seeking to halt 'Wildwood' screenings at L.A.’s Bruin Theatre, citing concerns about operator Rui Pereira.
entry.content:
L.A.’s historic Bruin Theatre met its ambitious fall reopening target on Friday, October 23, but its return is already facing a challenge from the companies behind its first attraction. Laika and Fathom Entertainment say they have taken legal action to stop the Bruin from showing “Wildwood.”

The film was previously advertised as a week-long run at the newly reopened Westwood venue. But in a joint statement provided exclusively to IndieWire, the animation studio and its theatrical distribution partner said concerns about operator Rui Pereira‘s history of controversial comments and behavior prompted them to seek an end to screenings.

Related Stories
‘Elastic Hearts’ Filmmakers Claim Their Movie Was Denied a Texas Tax Incentive Over Abortion Storyline
Why Emmy Wins and Hollywood Recognition Don’t Guarantee Jobs for BIPOC Artists: ‘The Needle Has Not F***ing Moved’

“When Laika became aware of the Bruin engagement, we immediately raised concerns with Fathom Entertainment, our theatrical distribution partner. Laika and Fathom commenced legal action to end the film’s screenings at the theatre,” the companies said in an email.

“We have not yet received confirmation that the screenings have stopped. We are continuing to explore our options, as the concerns regarding the theatre operator are incompatible with the values of our two companies.” IndieWire independently confirmed that “Wildwood” screenings had continued at the Bruin through at least Sunday afternoon, October 25, and as of publication, the theater’s website still advertised daily screenings at 1:30 p.m., 4 p.m., 7 p.m., and 9:30 p.m.

Laika and Fathom Entertainment did not specify what kind of legal action they had taken to stop showings of their film. On a phone call with IndieWire, Pereira asked how we had obtained a cease-and-desist letter. IndieWire had neither received nor reviewed such a letter and told Pereira we had communicated directly with the companies. He continued, “You guys are assholes. Everything you have written is false.”

The dispute introduces an immediate programming problem for Pereira’s revived movie palace, which reopened with “Wildwood” after sitting dark since Regency Theatres departed the space in July 2024. It also follows months of scrutiny involving Pereira, whose rocky history operating Toronto’s Kingsway Theatre became the subject of an IndieWire investigation on September 3.

IndieWire’s earlier reporting examined allegations of assault, nonpayment, racial discrimination, online harassment, and unauthorized film exhibition. The reporting drew on interviews with more than 25 sources in the U.S. and Canada, as well as court records, digital correspondence, social media posts, and years of advertised Kingsway screenings some rights holders say they did not authorize. Pereira has broadly disputed those allegations and characterized the ongoing scrutiny of his businesses as an effort to undermine his work as an exhibitor.

“There are no controversies and any attempt to generate them is dishonest and disingenuous,” Pereira said then. “The Bruin Theater is a gift, not only to Los Angeles, but the world — a cultural heritage site that unites generations of movie goers in the experience of cinema.”

Several journalists have described being targeted by Pereira after publishing critical coverage or omitting the Kingsway from their reporting. Speaking with IndieWire on the phone and in a subsequent email on October 26, Pereira referred to IndieWire staff as “presstitutes” and accused the publication of getting paid to write about him negatively.

Two volunteers left the Bruin restoration project in August after posts attributed to the Kingsway account circulated among Los Angeles moviegoers. Screenshots reviewed by IndieWire included racist and antisemitic remarks, as well as exchanges targeting individual patrons. Sources also described threats and a pattern of prolonged retaliation, alleging that Pereira continued targeting some critics online for months or years after their initial disputes.

When asked by The Hollywood Reporter in an August 23 report about some specific Kingsway posts — including one telling a target to “Go back to Poland” and another describing a swastika painted on a Jewish family’s home as “the proper symbol for zionazis” — Pereira acknowledged that the comments were “offensive” and said he “must take responsibility.”

The current dispute over “Wildwood” also follows separate questions about the Kingsway’s programming. IndieWire previously identified 55 advertised screenings of 17 films that three rights holders said they had not authorized at Pereira’s Toronto theater. Those findings came from a limited sample and did not establish that all or even most Kingsway screenings were unlicensed. “There are no issues with film licensing or any disputes,” Pereira said previously.

Notably, Laika and Fathom’s statement does not suggest that the Bruin’s “Wildwood” booking was unauthorized from the outset. Rather, the companies say they sought to end the Bruin screenings over specific concerns about Pereira as operator. “Wildwood” opened in nearly 3,000 theaters nationwide, and a booking on that scale is hardly an endorsement of every exhibitor.

Still, independent theaters often build their identities around the taste and reputations of the people running them. At a beloved landmark like the Bruin, affection for an old movie palace can translate into intense trust in whoever promises to save it. For now, the location has achieved the reopening its new operator promised. Whether it can continue showing the film that brought audiences back is in dispute.

entry.title: ‘Elastic Hearts’ Filmmakers Claim Their Movie Was Denied a Texas Tax Incentive Over Abortion Storyline
entry.summary: Indie film 'Elastic Hearts' was denied a tax credit after filming in Texas over what the filmmakers claim were political reasons tied to abortion.
entry.content:
Filmmaker Milad Avaz hoped his movie might ruffle some feathers and start a conversation, but he never expected it would create controversy as he was making it.

Avaz is a Danish-Iranian filmmaker based out of Copenhagen who last year shot his first English-language feature titled “Elastic Hearts.” The indie film stars Cole Sprouse, Darby Lee-Stack, Dean Norris, and Stephen Dorff, and after experiencing how many films are always fighting for competition in Los Angeles, he and his brother, producer Misam Avaz, decided to shoot somewhere else: Texas.

The location made narrative sense, too. The film follows a 19-year-old cello prodigy living in a rural part of Texas who turns to her gay, estranged older brother for help when she discovers she’s pregnant. That prompts the two of them to travel out of state to visit an abortion clinic. But “Elastic Hearts” is more concerned with grief and family coming together than abortion rights in Texas, where the procedure has been largely outlawed since 2022.

Related Stories
Why Emmy Wins and Hollywood Recognition Don’t Guarantee Jobs for BIPOC Artists: ‘The Needle Has Not F***ing Moved’
From ‘The Devils’ to ‘Obsession,’ How ‘Femcel’ Horror Handles Horny Women

The Avaz brothers were not naive to that fact when they chose Texas as a shooting location and when they applied for a grant through the Texas Moving Image Industry Incentive Program (TMIIIP), which can net filmmakers up to a 31 percent tax credit in grant money for eligible productions. They were also not naive to Texas rules for eligibility, which award grant funds after production, not before, and which explicitly state that the Texas Film Commission may deny any application “because of inappropriate content or content that portrays Texas or Texans in a negative fashion.” But after working closely with the Texas Film Commission and Austin Film Commission for months during pre-production, they thought the credit was a sure thing.

So they were shocked to learn that after an abnormally long delay, their application was rejected; no formal reason was given in writing. Avaz claims, though, that in a subsequent call with someone at the film commission who was equally shocked, he and his brother say “Elastic Hearts” was denied a grant for political reasons following a closed-door meeting directly from the office of Texas Governor Greg Abbott. It was what was said to them at the end of the call that floored them most.

“You made a film about abortions in Texas. What did you expect?”

“It was so blatant that political influence and government elected officials had an influence on what art was being created that we were just baffled by it,” Milad Avaz told IndieWire exclusively. “I definitely think that’s why it was denied. So when you ask me, what do you think are the themes that led to this, I can tell you pretty upfront that it’s the abortion rights.”

Texas’ film credit program has very recently become a political football after a Texas House representative called the program a “socialist scheme” and vowed to repeal it after a star of “The Chosen” endorsed Democrat James Talarico in the looming U.S. Senate election. It’s also not the first time the Texas Film Commission has denied a credit. In 2019, Robert Rodriguez (who is about as Texan as it gets) unsuccessfully sued after his application for a grant on “Machete Kills” was twice denied.

What makes the case of “Elastic Hearts” shocking though, is how an indie film that used a largely Texan crew was not just denied but had the rug pulled out from under them after the movie was completed. Avaz feels his rejection is a chilling example of what can happen when politics influences art.

“I’m not naive. I know the outcome of this decision fits very well with the political climate, both in America and in the world right now. I just do not think we should be okay with this,” Avaz said. “I don’t think this should be something that, oh well, this is the time where political leaders decide what art is made, so we’re not going to really focus on it. This needs to be documented that we live in a time where, in our industry that is really struggling in a lot of ways, we also have to deal with the very little money available for us independent filmmakers being withheld for political reasons. We have some of our heroes in the film industry doing commercials for ‘Come to Texas, film here!’ Just don’t make it political in any way.”

“It shouldn’t be like this when you do movies,” Milad’s brother Misam Avaz said. “As a movie maker, you should have the right when you use your voice to tell something this important, you should have that freedom of speech. I think it’s a thing that we need to do something about. I asked Milad, and he had the same feeling that I had in the guts, this is not right.”

“Elastic Hearts” carried a $2.2 million budget, and the film’s application, which was filed ahead of the film’s start of production on September 8, 2025, outlined an estimated $1.24 million in planned Texas spending (Avaz said the spending was closer to $1.3 million). Avaz was informed the turnaround time for the application generally lasts 1-3 months, but they did not receive a formal response until nine months later on June 25, 2026, well after production in Texas had wrapped. The film has now already completed post-production and has submitted for consideration at Sundance and South By Southwest (if Avaz is allowed back in the state after this incident, he jokes).

Avaz described the formal response via email, which IndieWire has obtained, as vague and succinct to the point that it felt like they were canceling lunch plans, not rejecting a grant worth over a hundred thousand dollars. When the application was denied and they asked for an explanation, Avaz found them unwilling to supply a reason in writing. It was not until August that they were able to get their representative from the Texas Film Commission to speak to them on the phone, at which point they were told the governor’s office reviewed the film for its political content as part of a closed-door meeting at which their rep was not permitted. When asked if they could appeal or apply again, they were told it wouldn’t make a difference.

In a statement to IndieWire, Governor Abbott’s Press Secretary Andrew Mahaleris said, “Under Texas law, the office is not required to act on every grant application and reviews each application thoroughly. In making determinations, the office considers general standards of decency and respect for the diverse beliefs and values of the citizens of Texas. The State does not use taxpayer dollars to fund projects that portray Texas or Texans in a negative fashion.”

The written application for “Elastic Hearts” does not explicitly mention abortion as part of the film’s story but describes the film as about two siblings who, “haunted by the recent loss of their mother, and carrying the weight of unresolved grief, the two navigate a fractured relationship marked by love, guilt, and buried pain. As they move through dusty towns, desert highways, and chance encounters with strangers, the journey forces them to confront the past and redefine their sense of family.”

The application does note, however, that in addition to hiring a local crew of 40+ people, as well as about 125 background actors, “Elastic Hearts” is a “tribute to and reimagining of Texas,” one that, with some international distribution deals already secured, will have a global reach for the state’s tourism.

“The film captures the textures of rural towns, long desert roads, neon-lit motels, and the quiet strength found in the everyday rhythms of the state. With locations ranging from Elgin to beautifully made minimalistic churches, Texas becomes more than a backdrop. It is woven into the emotional and visual fabric of the story,” the application reads in part. “Texas is not just a backdrop but a central part of the film’s emotional and visual identity, influencing the tone, atmosphere, and character relationships throughout the story.”

Avaz argued too that the film’s story isn’t black and white in its ideas about abortion. It’s a movie about a young woman making a difficult decision because she knows either choice — to keep the child or terminate the pregnancy — might be right for her.

“I needed to show this place from a place of love. There was no way this was going to represent Texas in a wrong light or in a negative way because I didn’t view Texas in a negative way,” he said. “I love the place. Me and my family lived there for half a year, and we want to go back. The response I also got from the crew was that we’re doing something they felt was important and they could really stand behind this project.”

“Elastic Hearts” stood to earn a credit of about $128,000, according to Misam, which came from a base credit of 10 percent based on their amount of spend, as well as a small additional credit for shooting in rural locations. The money would’ve effectively covered the post-production budget, and as a result it hurts the backend they can earn from this film and impacts their ability to start on the next project on their slate. They’re stable as a company after this, but it easily could be something that would ruin another filmmaker or first-time director.

Avaz said everyone involved was riled up based on the decision, and in statements to IndieWire, both of the stars Sprouse and Lee-Stack made that outrage clear.

“By all criteria our film qualified for the state’s film incentive, and if what we’ve been told is true, then the denial of our application is a constitutional violation of the First Amendment and more plainly — viewpoint discrimination,” Sprouse said. “Our jobs as artists often intersect with existing social and political boundaries, and it’s our duty to fight against the erasure of those suffering within this broken system. If the news of denial on these grounds is legitimate, then I’m deeply disappointed by both the cowardice of the Texas Film Commission and not surprised in the slightest by Governor Abbott.”

“Censorship. That is what it says. This is yet another attempt to control our freedom of choice and speech in the U.S,” Lee-Stack added. “This decision made by one politician on behalf of all Texans robs Texas of an opportunity to represent itself as a community of diverse thought and culture. This film is not just about one issue. At the core of ‘Elastic Hearts’ is a reflection of the state’s natural beauty and the admirable resilience of its people. Independent film — the epitome of our freedom of speech and self-expression — should not be controlled by politicians. Regardless of this attempt, I believe this film will reach who it needs to reach because it is too relevant and necessary to be stifled.”
